title: Set a boring bar in the lathe tool block: tip to the chuck, 45-64 mm out
instruction: Set the boring bar in the tool block to bore the 40 mm deep hole: lay it in the block's channel, gold insert up and its tip toward the chuck, sticking out past the block's face far enough to reach the full depth with 5 mm to spare (at least 45 mm) but no more than four times its 16 mm shank (64 mm). Keep the tip off the part.
context: Machinists set a boring bar's overhang at every lathe setup that bores a hole. The rule is the shortest stick-out that still reaches the bottom of the bore with a little to spare, and never more than about four times the shank size for a steel bar: chatter and deflection grow steeply with overhang, so a long bar leaves a rough, oversize bore, while a short one lets the tool block hit the part before the bore is finished. The bar must also face the chuck with its cutting insert up, or it cannot cut. The setter lays the bar in the tool block, checks the overhang with a steel rule from the block's face to the tip, then clamps it.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. A bench-scale lathe mock is laid out with its spindle axis along y at x 25.0 cm, 48 mm above the table. Everything except the bar is fixed to the table. (1) Tool block: a dark steel block 50 mm (x) by 80 mm (y), 40 mm tall, spanning x 22.5-27.5 cm and y -8.0 to 0 cm. Its face toward the chuck (the +y face, at y 0) is the block face the stick-out is measured from. Two dark steel walls, 12 mm thick, 80 mm long and 12 mm tall, run along its top in y at its two edges, leaving a 26 mm wide channel along y (x 23.7-26.3 cm) whose floor is the block's top, 40 mm above the table. (2) Chuck: a grey steel block 100 mm (x) by 30 mm (y), 96 mm tall, at x 20.0-30.0 cm, y 11.5-14.5 cm. (3) Workpiece: an aluminium block 50 x 40 x 50 mm (40 mm along y) held in the chuck, spanning x 22.5-27.5 cm, y 7.5-11.5 cm and 23-73 mm above the table, centred on the spindle axis. Its face toward the tool block is at y 7.5 cm, 75 mm from the block face. (4) Bore mark: a black 22 x 22 mm square of tape (0.5 mm thick here), on that face, centred on the spindle axis: the mouth of the 40 mm deep bore. (5) Tool mat: black rubber, 180 mm (x) by 60 mm (y), 3 mm thick, centred at x 19.5 cm, y -17.0 cm. (6) Boring bar, loose: a 16 x 16 mm square bar 150 mm long, 0.30 kg, made of a 135 mm steel shank, a 15 mm black-oxide steel head of the same section at its tip end, and a gold (TiN-coated carbide) cutting insert, 6 x 6 mm and 3 mm tall, on top of the head, centred across it and flush with the tip face. It lies on the mat along x, centred at x 19.5 cm, y -17.0 cm, insert up, its tip toward +x (away from the arms), the tip face at x 27.0 cm. A bar lying in the channel has its centre line at the spindle axis height and touches the workpiece when its tip is 75 mm past the block face; it balances on the block face's edge at a stick-out of about 75 mm, so in every position the scoring counts (up to 72 mm) it rests on the block by itself. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: End state, read at the last step from the bar's pose (in a real trial: a steel rule, a top photo and a look from the side). 'Stick-out' s is how far the centre of the bar's tip face is past the block face, along the spindle axis (y), in mm (negative if the tip is inside the block). 'At rest': neither end of the bar has moved more than 2 mm in the last 0.5 s. 'In the channel': the bar lies insert up, tilted 5 degrees or less (the axis through the insert within 5 degrees of vertical: a bar pitched, rolled, on its side, insert down or on an end is tilted), its axis within 10 degrees of y seen from above, with at least 20 mm of its length over the block, and at both ends of that part (the block's back face or the bar's back end, and the block face or the tip) its centre line is within 6 mm of the channel's centre line sideways (the bar has 5 mm of play either way; more means it is on a wall) and its underside within 3 mm of the channel floor. Score 0 if any of: (a) the bar is not at rest at the end; (b) it is not in the channel; (c) its tip points away from the chuck (the tip is its -y end); (d) s is more than 72 mm: the tip is less than 3 mm from the workpiece's face (2.5 mm from the bore mark) or touches the part. Otherwise, by the stick-out: 45 <= s <= 64 mm (reaches the 40 mm bore depth with 5 mm to spare, overhang at most four times the 16 mm shank): 1.0 (success, held at rest for 2.5 s); 38 <= s < 45 mm (less than the 5 mm to spare, at most 2 mm short of the 40 mm depth) or 64 < s <= 72 mm (past the four-times rule): 0.5; s < 38 mm (more than 2 mm short of the depth, including a tip inside the block): 0.25. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0; every pose at rest in the channel, insert up and tip toward the chuck, falls in exactly one tier by its stick-out, and each tier is a position the bar rests in by itself. The scorer sees only the bar, not the gripper: a bar held still in place is scored where it lies.
fidelity: Rigid bodies with the simulator's default friction. The lathe is a bench-scale mock of fixed boxes: no spindle, slides or clamp screws; the bar rests in the channel by gravity, and the bore is a mark. In a real trial nothing is powered and the insert is a dummy. The bar is one rigid body of three boxes with its mass spread evenly by volume (the 1 g insert is counted as steel). The scorer reads only the bar's pose, not the gripper.
reset_notes: Put the bar back on the black mat centred at x 19.5 cm, y -17.0 cm, lying along x with its tip toward +x (away from the arms) and the insert up. Nothing is consumed.
